question: What is the main use of an oxygen tent in children's wards?

options.B: Providing mechanical ventilation for adult trauma
options.C: Delivering controlled oxygen in pediatric care
options.D: Treating severe burn wounds in sterile isolation

explanation: Oxygen tents are super helpful in pediatric wards! They let us give steady oxygen to toddlers and young kids who might keep pulling off a standard face mask. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h1)

question: Why do nurses tuck the edges of an oxygen tent firmly under the mattress?

options.A: To anchor the heavy metal frame securely to the bed
options.B: To prevent the loss of the enriched oxygen atmosphere
options.C: To completely block all ambient light from the room
options.D: To keep the pediatric patient from crawling out of bed

explanation: Tucking the plastic sides under the mattress creates a nice seal so the oxygen stays inside with the child instead of leaking out into the room. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h1)

question: Which young patient is most likely to need an oxygen tent?

options.A: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in an adult
options.C: Decompensated heart failure with fluid overload

explanation: Spot on! Respiratory infections like bronchiolitis make it hard for little ones to breathe, making an oxygen tent a great choice to help them recover. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h2)

question: Why is an oxygen tent not the best choice when a patient needs very high oxygen levels?

options.A: The plastic material is chemically unable to hold high pressure
options.B: Opening the canopy to care for the patient causes the oxygen level to drop
options.C: Adults consume too much oxygen for the tent motor to handle
options.D: High oxygen levels melt the seals of the canopy frame

explanation: Every time you unzip or open the tent to check on the child or feed them, the trapped oxygen escapes quickly into the room air. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h2)

question: What is the job of the cooling unit attached to an oxygen tent?

options.A: Filtering bacteria out of the room air supply
options.B: Preventing the inside of the tent from becoming too hot
options.C: Increasing the pressure of oxygen inside the canopy
options.D: Freezing the oxygen gas into liquid form for storage

explanation: Because plastic tents trap body heat and humidity, the cooling unit is essential to keep the little patient comfortable and cool. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h3)

question: Which piece of equipment attaches to the oxygen source to control gas flow into the tent?
explanation: The flowmeter is your best friend for regulating the exact liters per minute of oxygen going into the tent system. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h3)

question: Why do we use high flow rates when running an oxygen tent?

options.A: To create positive pressure that forces fluid out of the lungs
options.B: To dry out excess moisture accumulating on the plastic
options.C: To speed up the cooling unit's internal fan blades
options.D: To flush out exhaled carbon dioxide and maintain oxygen levels

explanation: High gas flow keeps fresh oxygen coming in while pushing out the carbon dioxide the child breathes out, keeping the air safe inside. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h4)

question: What happens to the oxygen inside the tent right after a nurse opens the canopy?

options.A: It spikes to one hundred percent

explanation: Opening the tent lets the oxygen rush out into the wider room, causing a temporary drop in concentration until you seal it back up. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h4)

question: A nurse finds a toddler in an oxygen tent with damp clothes and cool skin. What should you do first?

options.A: Change the damp clothing and check the tent cooling settings
options.B: Administer an antipyretic medication for potential fever
options.C: Increase the oxygen flow rate on the wall flowmeter
options.D: Remove the child from the tent and place a nasal cannula

explanation: Moisture inside the tent can get clothes wet, which makes the child cold fast. Dressing them in dry clothes keeps them cozy and safe! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h5)

question: Which assessment is most important to keep checking for a patient in an oxygen tent?

options.A: Respiratory rate and work of breathing
options.C: Daily weight and fluid intake volume

explanation: Since oxygen tents treat breathing problems, always keep a close eye on how hard the child is working to breathe and their breathing rate. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h5)

question: Why are electrical toys not allowed inside or near an oxygen tent?

options.A: They interfere with the digital pulse oximeter readings
options.B: They can create small sparks that ignite the oxygen-rich air
options.C: They consume too much electricity from the hospital wall outlet
options.D: They make too much noise and frighten the pediatric patient

explanation: Oxygen feeds fire! Even a tiny spark from a toy motor can cause a serious fire hazard in an oxygen-rich space. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h6)

question: Which of these items is NOT safe to use inside an oxygen tent?

options.A: Silicone pacifiers used to soothe an infant
options.B: Plastic washable containers for holding water
options.C: Woolen blankets that generate static electricity
options.D: Cotton hospital gowns worn by the young patient

explanation: Woolen blankets create static sparks from friction, which is a major danger around high oxygen levels. Stick to cotton or safe materials instead! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h6)

question: What is a very common result of high humidity inside an oxygen tent?

options.A: Water condensation building up on the inner plastic walls
options.B: Sudden dropping of the room's overall humidity level
options.C: Freezing of the oxygen gas into solid ice crystals
options.D: Complete drying out of the patient's nasal passages

explanation: All that moisture in the enclosed space naturally turns into water droplets on the cooler plastic walls of the tent. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h7)

question: How can a nurse best stop a child in an oxygen tent from getting chilled by moisture?

options.A: Frequently dry the child's skin and change damp linens
options.B: Turn off the humidifier completely during the night shift
options.C: Apply petroleum jelly over the child's entire body
options.D: Open the canopy wide for one hour every morning

explanation: Regularly swapping out damp clothes and blankets prevents the moisture from chilling the child's body. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h7)

question: What should you check first if the oxygen level inside the tent suddenly goes down?

options.B: The expiration date of the plastic canopy
options.C: Tubing connections and canopy edge seals
options.D: The patient's blood pressure and heart rate

explanation: Always check your basics first! Loose tubing or edges that popped out from under the mattress are usually why oxygen is leaking out. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h8)

question: What should you do right away if the tent's cooling motor stops working during your shift?

options.A: Notify maintenance, monitor temperature closely, and provide temporary ventilation
options.B: Wrap the child in extra heavy blankets to prevent shivering
options.C: Increase the oxygen flow rate to maximum to cool the air down
options.D: Disconnect the oxygen entirely and move the child to a regular chair

explanation: A broken cooler will cause heat to build up inside. Call maintenance right away, keep an eye on the temperature, and fan or ventilate carefully to keep the child safe. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h8)
